trial_name: TTM2 — Hypothermia versus Normothermia after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2021)
citation: Dankiewicz J, Cronberg T, Lilja G, et al. Hypothermia versus Normothermia after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(24):2283-2294.
trial_type: RCT — international, multicenter, open-label with blinded outcome assessment, superiority
one_liner: In unconscious adults after OHCA, targeted hypothermia at 33°C did not reduce 6-month mortality or poor functional outcome compared to targeted normothermia with early fever treatment, but increased hemodynamic arrhythmias.

pico.population: Unconscious adults (≥18 years, FOUR motor score <4) admitted to ICU after OHCA of presumed cardiac or unknown cause with sustained ROSC (≥20 minutes), enrolled within 180 minutes of ROSC.
pico.intervention: Targeted hypothermia at 33°C for 28 hours followed by controlled rewarming (~0.33°C/hour) to 40 hours, mandatory sedation (0–40 hours), and active fever prevention (36.5–37.7°C) up to 72 hours if remaining comatose.
pico.comparison: Targeted normothermia with active device cooling triggered if core temperature reached ≥37.8°C (device target 37.5°C), mandatory sedation (0–40 hours), and active fever prevention (36.5–37.7°C) up to 72 hours if remaining comatose.
pico.outcome: Death at 6 months (primary outcome); poor functional outcome (mRS 4–6) at 6 months; safety outcomes including arrhythmias, pneumonia, sepsis, bleeding, and device-related skin complications.

background.existing_knowledge: Two early small 2002 RCTs reported improved survival and neurological outcomes with induced hypothermia (32–34°C) after witnessed shockable OHCA, leading to international adoption. The 2013 TTM trial found no difference between 33°C and 36°C, raising the hypothesis that clinical benefit stems from fever avoidance rather than active hypothermia.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty whether active cooling to 33°C provides any incremental clinical benefit over targeted normothermia with early treatment of fever in contemporary post-resuscitation care pathways.
background.hypothesis: Active induced hypothermia to 33°C with controlled rewarming improves survival and functional outcome compared with targeted normothermia with early fever treatment in unconscious adults after OHCA.

methods.design: International, multicenter, investigator-initiated, randomized, parallel-group, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment.
methods.setting: ICUs across multiple international centers; screening yield: 4355 screened, 1900 randomized (common non-randomization reasons: >180 min from ROSC n=794, non-cardiac cause n=441, not unconscious n=248, care limitations n=237). Enrolled June 2017 to January 2020.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU post-OHCA of presumed cardiac or unknown cause
Sustained ROSC (≥20 minutes without chest compressions)
Unconsciousness defined as inability to obey verbal commands (FOUR motor score <4)
Randomization within 180 minutes of sustained ROSC
Eligible for ICU care without limitations
exclusion: Severe COPD requiring long-term home oxygen therapy

methods.intervention: Hypothermia target 33°C. Intervention phase (0–40h) with mandatory sedation: Block A (28h) rapid cooling and maintenance at 33°C; Block B (12h) controlled rewarming at ~0.33°C/hour. Closed-loop intravascular or surface devices recommended; initial 4°C crystalloid ≤30 mL/kg permitted. If comatose after rewarming, maintained at 36.5–37.7°C until 72h post-randomization.
methods.comparison: Targeted normothermia. Device target 37.5°C with active device cooling triggered if recorded core temperature reached ≥37.8°C during first 40h. Antipyretics/conservative measures permitted. Same mandatory sedation framework (0–40h); if comatose, normothermic range (36.5–37.7°C) maintained until 72h post-randomization (plus 32h additional device fever control if device deployed).
methods.blinding: Open-label for temperature intervention to treating clinicians; 6-month functional outcomes assessed by blinded structured assessors; mortality is objective.
methods.sample_size_power: 1862 patients required to detect a 7.5% absolute reduction in 180-day mortality (55% to 47.5%, RR 0.86) with 90% power at 2-sided 5% significance level; planned enrollment 1900.
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality at 6 months (analyzed by intention-to-treat using generalized linear mixed modeling adjusted for site and TAME co-enrollment; Cox regression for survival).
secondary_outcomes: Modified Rankin Scale score at 6 months
methods.follow_up: 6 months for primary and functional outcomes.

headline_bullets: Targeted hypothermia at 33°C did not reduce 6-month mortality compared with targeted normothermia (50% vs 48%; RR 1.04; P=0.37).
Poor functional outcome at 6 months (mRS 4–6) was identical between groups (55% vs 55%; RR 1.00).
Hypothermia significantly increased arrhythmias causing hemodynamic compromise (24% vs 17%; RR 1.45; P<0.001).

outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome data missing for 11/1861 patients
Structured mRS missing/unstructured in 82/1747 assessed patients
Functional outcome unavailable in 21 patients (7 vs 14)
Survival analysis reported as hazard ratio

safety: Arrhythmia causing hemodynamic compromise: 24% (222/927) in hypothermia vs 17% (152/921) in normothermia (RR 1.45; 95% CI 1.21–1.75; P<0.001).
Device-related skin complications: 1% (10/927) vs 1% (5/922) (RR 1.99; 95% CI 0.69–5.74; P=0.20).

domains.notes: 1:1 ratio, central allocation concealment maintained prior to assignment. Stratified by site and TAME trial co-enrollment. Low selection bias risk given ≤180 minute enrollment window and objective eligibility criteria.

Open-label design (unblinded care teams); mitigated by standardized mandatory sedation framework (0–40h) in both groups. 6-month functional outcomes were assessed by blinded investigators; mortality is objective.

Of 1900 randomized, 39 excluded post-randomization (37 lack of consent/withdrawn, 2 double randomizations), leaving 1861 in ITT population (925 hypothermia vs 936 normothermia). Primary outcome data missing in only 11/1861 patients.

Median time to reach 34°C was 3 hours (IQR 2–4). Neuromuscular blockade within 72h used in 66% (586/892) hypothermia vs 45% (395/879) normothermia. Acetaminophen within 72h used in 58% (515/892) vs 71% (621/879). Median time to extubation or death was 3.7 days (IQR 1.4–7.7) vs 3.2 days (IQR 1.2–6.6). Median ICU LOS was 4.0 vs 3.6 days; hospital LOS 6.9 vs 6.5 days.

Well balanced: age 64±13 vs 63±14 years; male 80% vs 79%; bystander witnessed 91% vs 92%; bystander CPR 82% vs 78%; shockable rhythm 72% vs 75%; median time to ROSC 25 min in both; median time to randomization 136 vs 133 min; admission shock 28% vs 30%; lactate 5.9±4.4 vs 5.8±4.2 mmol/L.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong given rapid randomization, protocolized co-interventions and neuroprognostication at ≥96 hours, blinded functional assessments, and near-complete primary outcome follow-up, with main limitation being the open-label design.

domains.notes: Representative of adult ICU OHCA admissions in high-performing emergency systems (91–92% bystander witnessed, 78–82% bystander CPR, 72–75% shockable initial rhythm). Excludes unwitnessed asystole, pre-ROSC ECMO, intracranial hemorrhage, severe COPD on home O2, pregnancy, admission temp <30°C.

Directly applicable to ICUs with capacity for continuous core temperature monitoring, active cooling devices, and protocolized sedation/neuroprognostication. Compares 33°C to active fever prevention, not to unmonitored/unmanaged fever.

external_validity.verdict: Generalizability is high for adult OHCA patients admitted unconscious to ICUs capable of active fever control, but limited for in-hospital arrests, unwitnessed asystole, or low-resource settings lacking device-based temperature management.

strengths: Large pragmatic international trial evaluating contemporary post-cardiac arrest ICU care.
Active normothermia comparator with device-triggered cooling at ≥37.8°C isolates the specific effect of 33°C over active fever prevention.
Standardized 40-hour intervention protocol with mandatory sedation and delayed multimodal neuroprognostication at ≥96 hours to prevent self-fulfilling prophecy.
Blinded, structured assessment of patient-centered 6-month functional outcomes with near-zero primary outcome missingness.
limitations: Open-label intervention introduces risk of performance bias, reflected in higher neuromuscular blockade and longer mechanical ventilation in the hypothermia group.
Post-randomization exclusion of 39 patients due to consent issues or double enrollment departs slightly from pure intention-to-treat principles.
Evaluated a single target hypothermia temperature (33°C) and single duration profile; does not address alternative targets or cooling durations.
Comparator embedded active device-activated fever control, limiting inferences regarding complete absence of temperature management.

critical_appraisal.summary: Definitive, high-quality pragmatic trial proving that routine induced hypothermia to 33°C provides no survival or functional benefit over active normothermia and fever control in unconscious OHCA survivors, while increasing hemodynamic arrhythmias.
strengths: Active comparator isolating fever prevention from hypothermia
weaknesses: High proportion of witnessed shockable arrests limits generalizability to low-survival systems

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients who were unconscious after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, therapeutic hypothermia did not lead to lower mortality at 6 months than targeted normothermia.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine therapeutic hypothermia at 33°C should be de-implemented in favor of targeted normothermia with active fever prevention (target ≤37.5°C, treat ≥37.8°C).
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients admitted to the ICU unconscious following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac or unknown origin.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Temperature control is useless; active prevention and early treatment of fever remain an essential component of post-cardiac arrest care.
implementation_caveats: Requires continuous core temperature monitoring and active antipyretics/device cooling when core temperature reaches ≥37.8°C.
Formal neuroprognostication must remain delayed until at least 96 hours post-arrest.
Anticipate higher rates of hemodynamic arrhythmias if hypothermia is used.

controversies.topic: Active normothermia vs true unmanaged control
controversies.notes: TTM2 evaluated 33°C versus active normothermia with device cooling at ≥37.8°C, not 'cooling versus no temperature control'. The result proves no incremental benefit of 33°C over active fever prevention.
Excluding 39 patients post-randomization for consent or double randomization creates minor methodological tension with strict ITT principles, though unlikely to affect trial conclusions.
WLST decisions remain potential sources of bias in unblinded post-arrest trials; mitigated in TTM2 by strict protocolized neuroprognostication at ≥96 hours.

context_related_trials.relation: Showed no outcome difference between 33°C and 36°C; TTM2 extended this by testing 33°C against targeted normothermia with active fever control.
Early landmark RCTs establishing 32–34°C hypothermia; TTM2 showed these findings do not hold up against modern post-resuscitation care and active fever prevention.
Co-enrollment trial integrated with TTM2, used as a stratification variable in randomization.

unresolved_questions: Whether specific ultra-high-risk sub-phenotypes derive benefit from 33°C hypothermia.
The role and optimal target of active temperature management in in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) or primary non-shockable rhythms.
Optimal duration and method (pharmacologic vs device) of active fever control after resuscitation.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Targeted hypothermia at 33°C does not improve 6-month survival or functional outcomes over active fever control (≤37.8°C) in OHCA, and increases hemodynamic arrhythmias.
